record.label: Gradient martingale and the derivative of its second moment
record.statement: For gamma in U and its controlled diffusion X from support.diffusion, u=Phi_x satisfies u(t,X_t)=int_0^t Phi_xx(s,X_s)dB_s for t<1. Consequently q(t)=E[u(t,X_t)^2] is C1 on [0,1), q(0)=0, 0<=q<=1, and q'(t)=E[Phi_xx(t,X_t)^2], with the right derivative at 0. These moment functions converge uniformly under the compact-strip approximations.
record.boundary: Curated source-level mathematical statement, not an elaborated Lean extraction or independently accepted proof. Its displayed local hypotheses are quantified guards; a hypothetical plateau is not an added premise of the full-support theorem. The bound |u|<=1 and the zero-field symmetry are essential. This does not assert q(t)=t for an arbitrary admissible coefficient; that is a later consequence of minimality and full support.

aligned_passages.text: ### 10.3 The zero coefficient The admissible coefficient $\gamma_0=0$ makes the use of minimality in the normalization step explicit. Its diffusion is $X_t=B_t$, and the [zero-coefficient heat formula][fs-reg] gives $$ u_0(t,x)=2F_{\mathrm G}\!\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-t}}\right)-1, \qquad a_0(t,x)=\sqrt{\frac2\pi}\frac{e^{-x^2/(2(1-t))}}{\sqrt{1-t}}. $$ Since $\mathbb E e^{-\lambda B_t^2}=(1+2\lambda t)^{-1/2}$, $$ \mathbb E a_0(t,B_t)=\sqrt{\frac2\pi},\qquad \mathbb E a_0(t,B_t)^2=\frac2{\pi\sqrt{1-t^2}},\qquad q_0(t)=\frac2\pi\arcsin t. $$ The last identity follows by integrating $q_0'=\mathbb E a_0^2$ from $q_0(0)=0$. This heat and late-step variation argument is the zero-field specialization of [Chen, Handschy and Lerman, Theorem 6 and its proof, arXiv:1609.04368v4, pp. 13–16](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.04368v4). Strict convexity of $\arcsin$ gives $q_0(t)

## 3. How a candidate receives its value To rule out a candidate, we will look for an allowed change that lowers its value. Adding mass at one scale changes the cumulative coefficient at every later scale. We therefore need both a value for each candidate and a way to compute the cost of that change. The auxiliary optimisation below supplies the value; its response to the starting state will enter the first-variation formula in Section 5.1. ### 3.1 First evaluate the zero coefficient The variational problem assigns each $\gamma$ a value by a one-dimensional auxiliary optimisation. Its final reward at state $x$ is $|x|$: this is the best one-spin score $\max_{\sigma\in\{-1,1\}}x\sigma$. First take $\gamma=0$, when only noise changes the state. The imported control representation uses noise with variance rate $\xi''$ ([Auffinger–Chen, Theorem 2][auffinger-chen]). Our normalisation $\xi(t)=t^2/2$ gives rate one, so the noise is **Brownian motion** $B$: a continuous random path starting at zero. Its increments over disjoint time intervals are independent; over an interval of length $h$, an increment has the law of the centred Gaussian $\sqrt h Z$. Starting at time $t$ in state $x$, the remaining noise $B_1-B_t$ therefore has the law of $\sqrt{1-t}Z$. The expected final reward is $$ \Phi_0(t,x)=\mathbb E|x+\sqrt{1-t}Z| =\int_{\mathbb R}|x+\sqrt{1-t}z|\varphi(z)\,dz. $$ At $(t,x)=(0,0)$ this is the calculation already performed: $\Phi_0(0,0)=\sqrt{2/\pi}$. At $t=1$ no noise remains and the value is $|x|$. The function gives an expected payoff at a specified starting state; it is not a probability density. ### 3.2 Allowing a response to the noise For a general $\gamma$, a response can bias the future state, with a quadratic cost. Here the overlap scale $t$ plays the role of time; the path is auxiliary, not a motion of the spins. The noise is the Brownian motion introduced above. A **control** $\alpha_s\in[-1,1]$ chooses a response at each time using only noise already observed since the starting time. The whole deterministic schedule $\gamma$ is known, but future noise is not. A rule chosen in advance can still give different responses on different observed paths. To see why this matters, let a sign $W=\pm1$, each with probability $1/2$, be revealed after a single choice $v\in[-1,1]$. The expected score $|W+v|-v^2/2$ is $1-v^2/2$, maximised at $v=0$. A choice $v=W$ would score $3/2$, but uses information unavailable at the time of choice. The continuous control problem repeats decisions with this same restriction; the finite example only illustrates that restriction. For a starting position $x$, the value is $$ \Phi_\gamma(t,x)=\sup_\alpha\mathbb E\left[ \left|x+B_1-B_t+\int_t^1\gamma(s)\alpha_s\,ds\right| -\frac12\int_t^1\gamma(s)\alpha_s^2\,ds \right]. $$ Inside the absolute value, noise and the accumulated bias change the state before its final reward is paid. The second integral is the running control cost. The supremum chooses the best permitted rule; its formal information condition is progressive measurability. Expectation now averages over Brownian paths for a fixed $\gamma$, rather than over spin couplings. At $\gamma=0$ both control terms vanish, recovering Section 3.1. The **Parisi functional** subtracts an explicit correction from this optimised value: $$ \mathcal P(\gamma)=\Phi_\gamma(0,0) -\frac12\int_0^1t\gamma(t)\,dt. $$ The inner supremum chooses a response for fixed $\gamma$; the outer problem minimises $\mathcal P$ over $\gamma$. The ground-state Parisi formula and attainment give $$ P_*=\min_{\gamma\text{ admissible}}\mathcal P(\gamma). $$ Each candidate supplies an upper bound, and minimisation finds the sharpest one. This equality and attainment are external inputs from [Auffinger–Chen (2017), Theorem 1 and the proof of Lemma 3][auffinger-chen]; Gaussian concentration gives the expected-value form used here. The no-gap theorem assumes a minimiser and proves a property of it. The value $\mathcal P(0)=\sqrt{2/\pi}$ alone does not establish that the zero candidate minimises. ### 3.3 The response, the state and the averaged square First consider the value as a function of the starting state, holding $t$ and $\gamma$ fixed; we also write $\Phi=\Phi_\gamma$. For any permitted control, use the same responses to each Brownian history at two starting states $x$ and $y$. The costs are unchanged, and the triangle inequality bounds the change in the terminal reward by $|x-y|$. Taking the supremum over controls gives $$ |\Phi_\gamma(t,x)-\Phi_\gamma(t,y)|\le |x-y|. $$ The value is also **convex**: between two states its graph lies at or below the chord joining their values. Indeed, each fixed-control payoff is an average of translated absolute-value functions, hence convex. Its chord lies at or below the chord of the best endpoint payoffs; taking the supremum preserves that upper bound. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemmas 2.1–2.2][support-regularity] supply spatial differentiability below time one. Let $u(t,x)=\partial_x\Phi_\gamma(t,x)$ be the slope as the starting state changes. A small shift $\delta$ changes the best expected payoff by approximately $u(t,x)\delta$. Write $a(t,x)=\partial_{xx}\Phi_\gamma(t,x)$ for the rate at which that slope changes. The displayed bound gives $|u|\le1$, and convexity gives $a\ge0$. These are spatial derivatives: time is held fixed. For the zero coefficient, the slope can be computed directly. Put $F_{\mathrm G}(z)=\Pr(Z\le z)=\int_{-\infty}^z\varphi(y)\,dy$. Moving $x$ slightly raises $|x+\sqrt{1-t}Z|$ when the final state is positive and lowers it when the final state is negative. Consequently $$ u_0(t,x)=2F_{\mathrm G}\!\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-t}}\right)-1. $$ Differentiating the integral is legitimate: the difference quotients of the absolute value are bounded by one, and the Gaussian has zero probability of hitting its corner. Thus the slope is the probability of a positive final state minus the probability of a negative one. For general $\gamma$, the control theorem says that the slope response attains the value. To see why this is the right response, consider a short step of length $h$ from $(t,x)$. A response $v$ adds displacement $h\gamma(t)v$, whose first-order contribution to the continuation value is $h\gamma(t)vu(t,x)$. Its running cost is $h\gamma(t)v^2/2$. The response-dependent gain per unit time is therefore $$ \gamma vu-\tfrac12\gamma v^2 =\tfrac12\gamma u^2-\tfrac12\gamma(v-u)^2. $$ Since $\gamma\ge0$ and $|u|\le1$, $v=u$ attains its maximum. The optimised contribution $\gamma u^2/2$ also explains why a squared slope will enter the sensitivity to $\gamma$. The control theorem and the first-variation formula in Section 5.1 make these connections rigorous; the square completion alone does not justify differentiating an optimised value. The control representation and feedback are justified for integrable coefficients in [OpenAI (2026a), Lemmas 2.1–2.2][support-regularity]; see also [Auffinger–Chen, Corollary 2 and the extension after (13)][auffinger-chen]. We first fix $\gamma$ and obtain the deterministic value and slope by optimising the expected future payoff. We then use that slope as a rule along a random path. Computing an expected future payoff does not reveal future noise: at time $t$, the rule needs only $t$ and the state already reached. Following it generates the state $$ X_t=B_t+\int_0^t\gamma(s)u(s,X_s)\,ds,\qquad X_0=0. $$ This is the **associated diffusion**. The cited regularity theorem gives its existence and uniqueness for a fixed Brownian motion. The rule is called **feedback** because it uses the slope at the currently reached state. With $\gamma$ and $u$ supplied, a short forward step of length $h$ from state $x$ at time $t$, with $t+h<1$, is approximated by $$ x+h\gamma(t)u(t,x)+\sqrt h Z. $$ The response is evaluated before the fresh independent noise $Z$ is observed. This discrete approximation explains the order of operations; the integral equation defines the continuous process. Its drift accumulates through time, so even a jump of $\gamma$ does not make $X$ jump. Fix $\gamma$, follow a path to $X_t$, evaluate the slope there, square it, and average over paths. This defines a deterministic curve $$ q(t):=\mathbb E[u(t,X_t)^2]. $$ Here $\Phi_\gamma$ and $u$ are deterministic functions; $X_t$ and the response evaluated at it are random. Squaring before averaging retains the size of both positive and negative responses. \Needspace{22\baselineskip} **A calculation at half time.** For $\gamma=0$, $X_t=B_t$ and $B_{1/2}$ has the same distribution as $Z/\sqrt2$. We can average over paths by grouping them according to the state reached. At half time the reached state has density $e^{-x^2}/\sqrt\pi$. This density describes its **law**, assigning probability to positions on the real line. The law has total mass one even though the order-parameter measure $\mu_0$ is zero. The two measures describe different objects. Average $u_0(1/2,x)^2$ with this density. Substituting $x=z/\sqrt2$ gives $$ \begin{aligned} q_0(1/2) &=\int_{\mathbb R}(2F_{\mathrm G}(z)-1)^2\varphi(z)\,dz\\ &=\int_0^1(2v-1)^2\,dv=\frac13, \qquad v=F_{\mathrm G}(z),\quad dv=\varphi(z)\,dz. \end{aligned} $$ The response at zero is zero, but its mean square at the random state is $1/3$. Thus $q(t)=t$ is not automatic. Although every control is optimal at $\gamma=0$, $q_0$ uses the value slope $u_0$. Section 7.1 uses the whole curve to find a feasible decrease of $\mathcal P(0)$; a discrepancy at one time does not suffice. **Question 2: change the time and the future.** Still take $\gamma=0$ everywhere, but now set $t=1/4$. What variance has the state accumulated, and what variance remains in its future reward? Write the Gaussian integral for $q_0(1/4)$ without evaluating it. Now take $\gamma=0$ before $1/2$ and $\gamma=1$ afterward. Does that same integral still compute $q(1/4)$? Identify what remains unchanged and what must be recomputed. [Answer 2](#answer-2). The analytic facts needed in the proof are $$ q\in C^1([0,1)),\qquad q(0)=0,\qquad 0\le q(t)\le1, \qquad q'(t)=\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^2]. $$ Here $C^1$ means continuously differentiable, with derivatives at zero from the right. In particular, $q'$ stays continuous across jumps of $\gamma$. Spatial curvature controls the growth of the squared response. These facts hold for every admissible candidate and follow from [OpenAI (2026a), Lemmas 2.1–2.2][support-regularity]. The initial value has a direct symmetry explanation: reflecting the starting state, noise history and response rule together preserves reward and cost, so $\Phi_\gamma(t,x)$ is even in $x$. Hence $u(t,0)=0$, and the zero-field starting state $X_0=0$ gives $q(0)=0$. Section 7.2 explains the stochastic calculation for $q'$. In Section 5, $q(t)-t$ will determine the first-order cost of changing cumulative weight. An added mass persists at every later time, so its cost requires a tail integral.

\Needspace{11\baselineskip}

### 7.1 Why the zero candidate does not minimise

Return to the Gaussian value and slope from Section 3. With $\gamma=0$,
the state is $B_t$. Differentiating the slope once more gives

$$
X_t=B_t,\qquad
u_0(t,x)=2F_{\mathrm G}\!\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-t}}\right)-1,
\qquad
a_0(t,x)=\sqrt{\frac2{\pi(1-t)}}e^{-x^2/(2(1-t))}.
$$

A Gaussian integral gives
$\mathbb E e^{-B_t^2/(1-t)}=\sqrt{(1-t)/(1+t)}$. Substituting
into $q_0'=\mathbb E[a_0(t,B_t)^2]$ and integrating from zero yields

$$
q_0'(t)=\frac2{\pi\sqrt{1-t^2}},\qquad
q_0(t)=\frac2\pi\arcsin t.
$$

This recovers the half-time value $1/3$. It also shows that
$q_0(t)\to1$ while $q_0'(t)\to\infty$: convergence of a function
at one does not bound its derivative there.
The constant direction $\eta=1$ is admissible and adds an atom at zero.
Its cost is

$$
D\mathcal P(0)[1]
=\frac12\int_0^1\left(\frac2\pi\arcsin t-t\right)dt
=\frac14-\frac1\pi<0.
$$

So a small positive constant coefficient improves the zero candidate.
This calculation uses the heat and variation formulas, not a minimiser
hypothesis; see also [Chen–Handschy–Lerman, proof of Theorem 6][chl-optimality].

### 7.2 The value equation and the moment identity

At $t=1$ there is no noise or response left to accumulate, so the value
is $|x|$. At earlier times it includes the best remaining response.
Its partial differential equation (PDE) runs backward from that final value:

$$
\partial_t\Phi_\gamma
=-\frac12\left(\partial_{xx}\Phi_\gamma
+\gamma(t)(\partial_x\Phi_\gamma)^2\right),
\qquad \Phi_\gamma(1,x)=|x|.
$$

With the spatial derivatives $u$ and $a$ defined in Section 3.3,
the equation expresses
a recursive choice: choose a response for a short first step, then
use the best continuation from the state reached. At a continuity
point of $\gamma$, this gives the formal first-order relation

$$
\Phi_\gamma(t,x)
=\sup_{|v|\le1}\left\{
\mathbb E\Phi_\gamma(t+h,x+\gamma(t)vh+\sqrt hZ)
-\tfrac12\gamma(t)v^2h\right\}+o(h).
$$

Subtract the present value, divide by $h$, and Taylor-expand.
The identities $\mathbb EZ=0$ and $\mathbb EZ^2=1$ give

$$
0=\Phi_t+\tfrac12\Phi_{xx}
  +\sup_{|v|\le1}\gamma(t)(v\Phi_x-v^2/2).
$$

The square completion from Section 3.3 gives a supremum of
$\gamma u^2/2$, attained at $v=u$, and hence the stated PDE. This calculation explains the equation;
justifying the recursion and the Taylor expansion requires the
control representation and regularity results. See
[Auffinger–Chen, Theorem 2 and Corollary 2][auffinger-chen] for the zero-temperature
control formula and [Jagannath–Tobasco, Lemma 18][jt-control] for the
control method with finite-temperature terminal data. The extension after
Auffinger–Chen's Corollary 2 covers integrable coefficients. The regularity
used here is in
[OpenAI (2026a), Lemmas 2.1–2.2][support-regularity].

Itô's rule is the chain rule for Brownian paths. Along
$dX_t=b_t\,dt+dB_t$, the coefficient of $dt$ (the **drift**)
in a smooth $f(t,X_t)$ is
$f_t+b_tf_x+f_{xx}/2$, and its noise term is $f_x\,dB_t$.
Differentiate the PDE in $x$ and take $b_t=\gamma u$. The drift of
the slope cancels:

$$
du(t,X_t)
=\underbrace{(u_t+\gamma u u_x+u_{xx}/2)}_{0}\,dt
+a(t,X_t)\,dB_t.
$$

Thus $M_t=u(t,X_t)$ is a bounded **martingale**: its conditional
expected later value, given observations up to time $t$, is its present
value. Zero field gives symmetry and $M_0=u(0,0)=0$. Applying Itô's rule once more
to $M_t^2$ gives

$$
d(M_t^2)=2M_ta(t,X_t)\,dB_t+a(t,X_t)^2\,dt.
$$

The noise term has mean zero because its coefficient is nonanticipating
and bounded on each strip ending before one. Taking expectations and
integrating yields $q(t)=\int_0^t\mathbb E[a(s,X_s)^2]\,ds$,
which gives the asserted derivative. Since $\mathbb EM_t=0$,
$q(t)$ is also the variance of the slope response.

For each fixed $T<1$, the required spatial derivatives are bounded on
$[0,T]\times\mathbb R$, and step-coefficient and smooth-terminal
approximations justify the identities. The bounds depend on the coefficient
and strip. The PDE holds almost everywhere in time. These are not
bounds up to time one.
